paper_title: HOG-WAM: Improving Visual Robustness through Future Gradient Prediction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet visual corruption can disrupt the resulting policies. We introduce HOG-WAM, which adds future Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) as structural supervision derived directly from demonstration images. An auxiliary HOG diffusion transformer (DiT) module reads RGB features through asymmetric attention, allowing its objective to shape the visual representation used for control. The module is used only during training and removed at inference, preserving FastWAM's RGB-to-action architecture. We evaluate four controlled observation corruptions through a visual-corruption extension of RoboTwin, termed RoboTwin-Plus; HOG-WAM achieves the highest success among the compared policies under all four. Mixed-noise success increases from 78.86% to 82.86% relative to FastWAM, with comparable performance on clean scenes. On LIBERO Plus, overall success increases from 74.49% to 75.26%, with the largest gain under sensor noise, from 74.14% to 78.89%. Across four Franka tasks, average success increases from 40% to 59% under clean observations and from 17% to 24% under noisy observations. A representation ablation favors combining RGB observations with auxiliary HOG prediction over replacing RGB with HOG. These findings support future-gradient prediction as complementary supervision for visually robust control, with larger absolute gains on physical tasks than in simulation. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/HOG-WAM.

Introduction Robotic manipulation requires recognizing task-relevant objects and anticipating how their spatial relations change during interaction. Vision-language-action policies use pretrained visual and language representations to map observations to actions [5, 17, 40]. World-action models (WAMs) additionally learn to predict future observations, making demonstrated scene evolution source of policy supervi- *Corresponding authors. sion [3, 18, 35]. Fast-WAM [38], denoted FastWAM here, preserves this predictive objective during training while generating actions from the current observation at inference. The prediction target therefore determines which visual information this training objective emphasizes. RGB prediction supervises object structure together with color, texture, and illumination. These appearance cues help identify objects, but they also vary with lighting and sensor conditions while the manipulation goal remains unchanged. An RGB objective alone thus ties the learned features to appearance factors that can change at deployment. For placement, stacking, and insertion, local boundaries describe the image-space arrangement of objects and their surroundings. Requiring visual representation to predict these boundaries provides an explicit structural learning signal alongside RGB reconstruction. The question is how to introduce this signal while retaining the appearance information needed for language-conditioned control. Why gradients? Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) [10] summarize local edge orientations through spatial pooling and contrast normalization. MaskFeat [30] demonstrates that predicting HOG features in masked image and video regions can learn useful visual representations, identifying local contrast normalization as an important component. This motivates different prediction problem for manipulation: learning the gradient structure of future demonstration frames alongside actions. The target emphasizes where local intensity transitions occur and how they are oriented, making spatial organization explicit without object annotations or learned target generator. Why training-only supervision? descriptor useful for supervising representation need not replace its sensory input. Our HOG raster compresses orientation statistics and removes chromatic information; RGB retains cues for object identity and instruction grounding. In HOG-WAM, an auxiliary HOG diffusion transformer (DiT) reads RGB features through asymmetric attention, and its loss updates the RGB backbone. Action prediction remains independent of HOG tokens, allowing the auxiliary module to be removed at inference while retaining its effect on the learned RGB representation. We evaluate visual robustness on RoboTwin 2.0 [7], LIBERO Plus [13], and four Franka tasks. The physical experiments show larger absolute gains over FastWAM than the simulation averages, extending the evidence to manipulation with real camera observations. Our contributions are: deterministic future-gradient target that makes local structure an explicit supervision signal for world-action learning. An asymmetric coupling of RGB, HOG, and action DiT modules that transfers this supervision to the visual backbone while preserving RGB-based inference. Evidence from controlled visual-corruption tests and physical manipulation, together with representation ablation that supports complementary HOG supervision over RGB replacement. 2. Related work Generative models and robot policies. Transformers [11, 29] provide token-based architectures for visual learning, while diffusion models [16], latent diffusion [26], and DiTs [25] support conditional image generation. Flow matching [20] and rectified flow [22] learn velocity fields that transport noise toward data. Diffusion Policy [9] applies conditional denoising to action sequences. RT-1 and RT-2 [6, 40] scale observation-to-action learning, while Octo and OpenVLA [14, 17] provide generalist policies adaptable to new robot settings. The π0 family [4, 5] combines pretrained vision-language representations with continuous action generation and heterogeneous training data. HOG-WAM instead studies how the visual prediction objective within WAM can improve the representation used for control. Predictive learning for control. UniPi [12] derives actions from text-conditioned video plans, and GR-1 [31] jointly predicts future images and actions after video pretraining. Video foundation models such as Wan [27] supply visual dynamics priors for recent WAMs. DreamZero [35], LingBot-VA [18], and MOTUS [3] couple visual dynamics and action generation through joint models. FastWAM [38] separates future-video training from action inference. Our auxiliary target builds on this separation, changing what the RGB representation is trained to predict. 2 Structural supervision in world models. TesserAct [39] models RGB, depth, and normals, while Kinema4D [33] uses kinematic robot trajectories to condition RGB and point-map simulation. WAM4D [19] transfers geometric priors through future-depth readouts that are removed at inference. MaskWAM [36] uses mask prompting and prediction, FlowWAM [8] adopts optical flow as an action representation, and Robust-WAM [34] aligns action-stream features with semantic targets. DreamWAM [37] combines appearance, motion, geometry, and semantics. HOG-WAM complements these learned or task-specific targets with local gradient statistics computed directly from each demonstration frame. Masked prediction and gradient targets. The target representation determines the information emphasized by predictive objective. BEiT [2] predicts discrete visual tokens; MAE and SimMIM [15, 32] reconstruct pixels; VideoMAE [28] extends masked reconstruction to videos; and I-JEPA [1] predicts learned target embeddings. Simulation benchmarks assess controlled visual and task variations; four Franka tasks assess physical manipulation. 4.1. Experimental setup FastWAM provides the RGBaction baseline; HOG-WAM adds an auxiliary HOG DiT module during training. Both policies condition actions on RGB observations, language instructions, and proprioception. We train separate pair of policies for each benchmark, using the same demonstration collection within each pair. We report success rate (SR) using each benchmarks task-completion criterion. We also include the released RoboTwin-adapted π0.5 [4, 23] and MOTUS [3, 24] policies as additional baselines. All four models are evaluated on all 50 tasks, with 100 valid episodes per task in each of six conditions: clean, randomized, and the four corruptions defined in Sec. 4.2. Discussion The experiments favor assigning gradients and RGB different roles: gradients structure the learning objective, while RGB preserves the information available to the policy. The design combines MaskFeats use of HOG as predictive target [30] with removable structural readout in the manner of WAM4D [19], obtaining the supervision from deterministic local image statistics. Its gains concentrate under sensor noise and viewpoint changes. The physical results extend the evidence beyond rendered observations, with larger absolute gains than the simulation averages. Each domain uses its own demonstrations, so these results establish effectiveness in both simulation and physical manipulation. The HOG DiT is removed at inference, so both policies execute the same architecture with the same parameter count, and the benefit resides in the trained RGB and action weights. 6. Conclusion HOG-WAM adds deterministic future-gradient supervision to predictive policy learning through an auxiliary DiT module and asymmetric attention. The resulting policy improves average success on RoboTwin-Plus, LIBERO Plus, and four Franka tasks while preserving the FastWAM inference architecture. The representation ablation supports retaining RGB observations and using structural prediction as complementary supervision; the gain is clearest under sensor noise.

Training and evaluation details B.1. Training configurations The RoboTwin collection contains 27,500 demonstrations from 50 tasks: 50 clean and 500 randomized demonstrations per task. Both policies use the same trajectory-level split of 27,225 training and 275 validation demonstrations and eight independently noised action copies per visual sample. Training uses AdamW with peak learning rate 104, weight decay 102, and effective batch size 1,024 for five epochs; evaluation uses the final step-29,365 checkpoints. The learning rate warms up for 1,468 steps and then decays by cosine schedule to 106. The optimizer uses (β1, β2) = (0.9, 0.95), ϵ = 108, and gradient-norm clipping at 1.
